newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade bourse begins 1997 with tight liquidity.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade bourse begins 1997 with tight liquidity.

text.p: The Belgrade Stock Exchange (BSE) reported on Monday an 8.2 percent increase in its turnover during the week ending January 10.
Total turnover reached 25.032 million dinars ($4.8 million) in 134 deals, up from 23.134 million dinars in 148 transactions during the last week of December.
BSE reopened on January 8 amidst the dinar crisis, with the currency sinking to around 4.3 to the German mark from its pre-hoiliday 3.8 level.

Analysts attributed the plunge to a monetary expansion that took place over the eight-day New Year and Christmas holidays, when streets of Belgrade and many other towns in Serbia were flooded with freshly printed dinar banknotes.

Economists said the latest toppling of the dinar, the fourth since the new "super dinar" was launched in January 1994 in an attempt to save the country from hyperinflation running at 60 percent a day, was a deliberate move by the Serbian government to fill in its fiscal gap.
In the meantime, numerous bank insolvencies, devaluation fears and political instability weighed on the fledgling financial market.

"Nominally, turnover rose around eight percent during three working days of the last week, but liquidity of the banking sector remains tight and revolving old borrowing is the key feature of the market," one trader told Reuters.
Traders said liquidity slightly improved on Friday but not enough to reflect on the market performance.
Despite a shortage of funds, investors were reluctant to raise interest rates in order to make quick profit.

"Interest rates hover around an average 0.45 percent a day. Some try to charge more, but they find no matching demand. But overall, those who had dinars fled to hard currency instead of risking to invest," another trader said.
For the week ending January 10, the BSE reported the following details:
* Commercial bills traded 108 times for a volume of 15.873 million dinars.
* Treasury bills accounted fo 21 deals worth 1.808 million dinars.
Interest rates on commercial paper and treasury bills ranged between an annual 331 and 793 percent.

* The central bank short-term bonds, auctioned January 6, were traded twice for a total of 5 million dinars. Traders said bonds regained buyer interest on higher interest rate, raised to an annual 121.80 from 77.90 percent.
* BSE reported two deals in wheat selling forward contracts worth 1.851 million dinars.
"Wheat contracts attract investors again. Flour mills are small but regular clientele," BSE spokesman Milko Stimac said.

An analyst said flour mills needed to secure enough wheat in advance. "Last year proved that Yugoslavia does not produce enough wheat. Despite some official assurances that 1997 harvest will be much better, they want to buy on time." -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
